title: Lamb of God (Matthew 8:8)
hook: the bread is broken and all say Lord, I am not worthy, only say the word

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Great Amen and the Our Father. Your line was so be it, all of us. When did you say yes out loud? Day one hundred and sixteen.

Remember the Roman officer, the centurion, back on day thirty-nine? His servant was sick at home. Jesus offered to come. And this powerful man, used to giving orders, said no. Don't come. I'm not worthy to have you under my roof. You don't need to come. Just say the word, and he'll be healed. Jesus was amazed. He said he hadn't found faith like that anywhere. Two thousand years later, every single time Catholics go to communion, just before they walk forward, they say that soldier's words. A pagan officer's sentence, placed on the lips of the whole Church. Today: the Lamb of God.
screen: `THE CENTURION, DAY THIRTY-NINE.` → `I AM NOT WORTHY.` → `HIS WORDS, ON EVERY LIP.`

segments.voice: After the Our Father, people turn and offer each other a sign of peace, a handshake, a nod, a hug for family. Then the priest takes the large host and breaks it. That breaking is so old that the first Christians called the whole Mass the breaking of the bread. He drops a small piece into the chalice, bread and wine together again. And while he does, everyone sings: Agnus Dei. Lamb of God. In Latin: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. Twice. And the third time, instead of mercy: dona nobis pacem, grant us peace. Why a lamb? Because of John the Baptist. When he first saw Jesus coming toward him, he said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." His listeners would have thought of the Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt the night of freedom. Then the priest lifts the broken host and says John's words, and the people answer with the centurion's. In the Douay-Rheims the officer says: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." At Mass, one word changes. Not my servant. My soul. Catholics say it about themselves. It's honest: nobody earns this. And it's hopeful: you don't have to be worthy, only open. One word from him is enough.
screen: `PEACE, THEN THE BREAKING.` · `LAMB OF GOD, GRANT US PEACE.` · `JOHN SEES THE LAMB.` · `NOT MY SERVANT: MY SOUL.` · then, large: `ONLY SAY THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the centurion's words, for someone else. Settle, and breathe. The centurion didn't ask for himself. He asked for someone at home. Think of someone who needs healing today, in body or heart. If you pray, you can use his sentence with their name in it: Lord, I am not worthy, but only say the word, and they will be healed. If you don't pray, hold them in mind, and wish them whole. The bell holds the time.
Agnus Dei. Latin for Lamb of God: the song as the bread is broken, from John the Baptist's words about Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: only say the word. Today, notice where you feel unworthy of something good, and let it come anyway. Day one hundred and sixteen.

howItsDone: After the sign of peace the priest breaks the consecrated host while the congregation sings the Agnus Dei; he then raises it with John the Baptist's words, and all respond with the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, adapted to 'my soul shall be healed'.

fork.reveal: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." Jesus said he had not found such faith.

original.note: Latin: Lamb of God, the chant sung as the bread is broken.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle hymn about a lamb.
what it means: the song as the bread is broken, calling Jesus the Lamb who takes away sin, then the centurion's words before communion.
what a scholar hears: John 1:29 and the Passover lamb of Exodus 12; the chant is traditionally said to have entered the Roman Mass under Pope Sergius I, around 700.

notes: Douay-Rheims John 1:29 and Matthew 8:8 given from memory; confirm.
The English Agnus Dei is given as a translation of the Latin, not quoted from ICEL; 'who take away' matches the Latin second person.
The people's response at communion ('my soul shall be healed') is described, not quoted from ICEL.
Pope Sergius I (687–701) and the Agnus Dei: attributed by the Liber Pontificalis; confirm the trapdoor wording 'traditionally said'.
The centurion was day 39 ('Only say the word') on this path; the hook refers back to it.
Commingling (a fragment of the host placed in the chalice) described simply; confirm.
